Columbia Fishing

October 15, 2026

Current and upcoming fishing opportunities:

Angling for coho has been fair to good near the mouths of some tributaries.

Announcements

For the latest regulations, including in-season changes see the fishing regulation update page.

Forecasts for 2026 Columbia River Spring Chinook, Summer Chinook, Fall Chinook, Coho, and Sockeye are available here.

Fish consumption advisories

The Oregon Health Authority has issued consumption guidelines for parts of the Columbia River due to high levels of mercury and/or PCBs. Fish with these chemicals look, act, smell and taste like any other fish, so caution is important.

  • Bonneville Dam fish advisory
  • Safe fish choices for pregnancy and young children

Sign up for the latest information on boater access

Marine Board's Opportunities and Access Report incorporates information from federal and state agencies, local facility operators and fellow boaters to provide up-to-date information so boaters can decide where to recreate and what to expect this season. Subscribe to receive email updates.

Click here to find Columbia River regulation updates for salmon, steelhead, shad and sturgeon.

SALMON, STEELHEAD, AND SHAD

On Sunday's (10/11) flight, there were 157 boats and 17 bank anglers from Bonneville Dam to Tongue Point.

Gorge: Weekly checking showed seven coho kept, and 89 Chinook and seven jack Chinook released for 10 boats (32 anglers).

Troutdale: Weekly checking showed 19 coho and four jack coho kept, and 29 Chinook, six jack Chinook, six coho, and two jack coho released for 41 boats (69 anglers).

PDX to Warrior Rock Lighthouse: Weekly checking showed three coho kept, and six Chinook and one jack Chinook released for 11 boats (21 anglers).

Warrior Rock Lighthouse to Longview Bridge: Weekly checking showed 124 coho and 12 jack coho kept, and 39 Chinook, 10 jack Chinook, and two jack coho released for 90 boats (239 anglers); and no catch for two bank anglers.

Longview Bridge to West Puget Island: Weekly checking showed 13 coho and one jack coho kept, and one Chinook released for four boats (nine anglers); and one jack coho kept for one bank angler.

West Puget Island to Tongue Point: Weekly checking showed no catch for two boats (four anglers).

Buoy 10: Weekly checking showed 47 coho kept, and 18 coho and two Chinook released for 92 boats (252 anglers); and two coho kept and one coho and one Chinook released for 47 bank anglers.

Bonneville Pool: Weekly checking showed 32 coho and two jack coho kept, and 134 Chinook, eight jack Chinook, and three jack coho released for 46 boats (117 anglers).

The Dalles Pool: Weekly checking showed one coho kept, and four Chinook released for four boats (nine anglers).

John Day Pool: Weekly checking showed six Chinook, two coho, and one jack coho released for eight boats (17 anglers); and no catch for one bank angler.

STURGEON

Lower Columbia River: Weekly checking showed one sub-legal and five over-legal sized white sturgeon released for one boat (two anglers).

Bonneville Pool: No report.

The Dalles Pool: Weekly checking showed no catch for one bank angler.

John Day Pool: No report.

WALLEYE

Lower Columbia River (below Bonneville Dam): No report.

Bonneville Pool: No report.

The Dalles Pool: Weekly checking showed no catch for one boat (one angler).

John Day Pool: Weekly checking showed 21 walleye kept, and two walleye released for 10 boats (22 anglers).

zones.html:
MARINE FISHING

October 15, 2026

Announcements

As of Jan 1, 2026, an Ocean Endorsement is needed for most recreational anglers fishing in the ocean. Check the Ocean Endorsement page for more information.

Report unusual fish and ocean conditions

Have you encountered unusual fish or ocean conditions off the Oregon Coast this year? With warm El Niño waters pushing up the coast, we're starting to see unusual tropical visitors migrating north! Report your on-the-water observations to CaCurrent.Observations@noaa.gov (more information available here). Your observations are critical to understanding how changing ocean conditions affect what we see offshore.

Saltwater News Bulletins

Be among the first to know about in-season changes! You can subscribe to receive emails and text message alerts for marine topics that interest you. It's easy to unsubscribe at any time. Your contact information will remain confidential. Three different lists of interests to ocean enthusiasts are available: bottomfish, halibut and ocean salmon.

Bottomfish

A few reminders

  • Visit the sport bottomfish seasons page to see what's new for 2026.
  • Retention of quillback rockfish and yelloweye rockfish remains prohibited.
  • Cabezon is prohibited from Jan 1 through June 30.

Port by port reports for the week beginning Oct 5:

Last week, most of the coast experienced typical fall transition conditions, with large swell limiting the number of good days to get out on the water.

Garibaldi: Anglers landed 3.2 rockfish on average, mostly black rockfish. Lingcod landings were slow at 0.27 fish per angler.

Depoe Bay: Landings averaged 3.4 rockfish per angler, with mostly black rockfish landed. Lingcod catches were slow at 0.25 fish per angler.

Newport: Anglers landed 3.6 rockfish per person, mostly black, deacon, and yellowtail rockfishes were observed. Lingcod was slow.

Charleston: Anglers landed near limits of rockfish, consisting of mainly black and yellowtail rockfishes. Lingcod was slow at 0.5 fish per angler.

Brookings: Anglers caught 1.5 rockfish on average; mainly black rockfish were landed. Lingcod was fair at 1 fish per angler.

The offshore long-leader fishery gives anglers an opportunity to catch more fish and to distribute effort away from nearshore species. Learn more about gear and the fishery.

Bottomfish fishing resources:

  • What can I keep and how many? Keep up with in-season regulation changes.
  • Know what you've caught with some helpful rockfish identification tips (including online quizzes and video).
  • Waypoints for fathom lines and other restricted areas.

Ocean salmon

Reminder: Ocean salmon anglers are reminded that they are limited to one rod, and no more than two single point, single shank, barbless hooks (no treble hooks) and that retention of jack salmon is not allowed in the ocean.

Leadbetter Point, WA to Cape Falcon, OR

Ocean salmon fishing is closed in the recreational fishery in the area from Leadbetter Point, Washington to Cape Falcon, Oregon. Possession of salmon on board a vessel is prohibited in the Columbia River Subarea.

Cape Falcon to Humbug Mountain

Cape Falcon to Humbug Mountain remains open through October 31, 2026, for all salmon except coho, with a daily bag limit of 2 salmon. The minimum size limit for Chinook is 24".

Humbug Mountain to the OR/CA border

The area from Humbug Mountain to the Oregon/California border is closed to ocean salmon fishing for the remainder of the year.

Ocean salmon fishing resources:

  • Keep track of where salmon catch and quotas are at north of Cape Falcon and south of Cape Falcon
  • See the ocean salmon regulations in either a time and area graphic view or as a map

Pacific halibut

See Pacific halibut season dates or visit the sport halibut page for more information.

Port by port reports for the week beginning Oct 5:

Newport was the only port with halibut trips observed and the average was 0.25 halibut per angler.

Shore and estuary fishing

Daily bag limits, seasons and licensing requirements for shore-based anglers are the same as for boat-based anglers.

There are plenty of rocky or sandy fishing sites up and down the coast where shore anglers can drop a line for saltwater fish. Read about how and where

Lingcod and many other bottomfish species are available year-round to shore anglers fishing in rocky areas. A common setup for lingcod is a jig head with a rubber swim bait – it's simple but effective. Also pack a measuring device for lingcod: the minimum legal size is 22 inches.

Surfperch are available in the surf year-round along sandy beaches and rocky shores, with the best fishing (and safest fishing) occurring when swells are small. Find surfperch and other learn to fish workshops and events here.

Want more opportunities that don't include a boat? Check out the crabbing and clamming recreation report for updates on crabs, clams, mussels and more!

When fishing from shore or inside estuaries and bays, it is important to check the tide. Many fish that swim into estuaries and bays, including salmon, surfperch, and Pacific herring, tend to come in with the tide. Catch of these species is more likely to occur closer to slack tide. Additionally, the accessibility of some areas can be completely dependent on the tide. Do not allow the incoming tide to become a safety issue.
